task: Argue whether a small bakery should raise prices by 10%.
consensus: Raising prices is risky. Bakery customers are price sensitive and nearby shops sell similar bread. Flour costs rose 8% this year, but a price hike could push regulars to competitors. A safer path is to keep prices and cut waste: day-old bread sells at half price, and unsold loaves currently run 12% of output. Cutting that to 6% offsets most of the flour increase. So the bakery should hold prices.
contrarian: Raising prices is the better choice. Bakery customers are price sensitive and nearby shops sell similar bread. Flour costs rose 8% this year, and cutting waste alone, from 12% of output to 6%, offsets most but not all of that. Regulars buy on habit and location, and a 10% hike on a $5 loaf is 50 cents. Losing under 9% of volume still leaves revenue flat or higher. So the bakery should raise prices.

task: Should a team of five engineers adopt microservices for a new product?
consensus: No. With five engineers, each service adds deployment, monitoring and network failure cases. The product is new, so boundaries between parts will move, and moving a boundary between services costs far more than moving one between modules. A modular monolith keeps the option to split later. The team should start with a monolith.
contrarian: Yes, for this team. With five engineers, each service adds deployment, monitoring and network failure cases, but their platform already provides those as managed tools at near zero setup. The product has two parts with very different scaling: video processing and a small web app. Splitting just those two lets the heavy part scale alone. The team should start with two services.

task: Is it worth learning to touch type as an adult programmer?
consensus: Yes. Typing speed rarely limits programming, but looking at the keyboard breaks focus many times a day. Touch typing takes about 20 hours of practice to pass a hunt-and-peck speed. That cost repays within months through fewer interruptions. Programmers should learn it.
contrarian: Usually not. Typing speed rarely limits programming, and a programmer who already types 60 words per minute while looking is not breaking focus in a measurable way. Touch typing takes about 20 hours of practice to pass that speed, and many people get slower for weeks. That time is better spent on reading code. Most programmers at 60 words per minute should skip it.

task: Should a city make public buses free?
consensus: Yes. Fares cover about 20% of this city's bus costs, and collecting them adds boarding delay. Free buses raised ridership 20 to 30% in similar cities. The lost fare revenue is small next to the gain in access for low-income riders. The city should make buses free.
contrarian: No. Fares cover about 20% of this city's bus costs, and collecting them adds boarding delay. Free buses raised ridership 20 to 30% in similar cities, but most new riders switched from walking and cycling, not cars. The same money spent on running buses more often would cut waiting time, which surveys rank above price. The city should keep fares and add service.

task: Should a beginner investor pick individual stocks?
consensus: No. Most professional fund managers fail to beat a broad index over 15 years. A beginner has less information and pays more per trade in time. A low-cost index fund gives market returns with little effort. Beginners should use index funds.
contrarian: A small slice, yes. Most professional fund managers fail to beat a broad index over 15 years, so the core of the money should sit in an index fund. Putting 5% into a few chosen stocks costs little in expected return and teaches how companies and valuations work faster than reading does. Beginners should hold index funds plus a small learning slice.

task: Is remote work better for junior employees?
consensus: No. Juniors learn by overhearing and asking quick questions. Remote work makes each question a scheduled message, so juniors ask fewer of them. Studies of software teams found juniors in the office got more feedback. Juniors should work in the office.
contrarian: It depends on the team, and often yes. Juniors learn by overhearing and asking quick questions, and remote work makes each question a written message. But written questions and answers stay searchable for the next junior, and teams with a habit of open chat channels gave juniors as much feedback as offices did. Juniors on teams with that habit can work remotely.
